clinicalPearls: Abrupt onset and rapid extension of symmetrical velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in flexures (neck, axillae, groin) in a non-obese, often older adult should prompt an urgent malignancy search.
Overwhelmingly associated with intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma; gastric carcinoma accounts for the majority, with pancreatic, colorectal, hepatobiliary and ovarian primaries also reported.
Mucosal and mucocutaneous involvement (oral cavity, lips, conjunctiva, anogenital) and periorbital or palmar disease are far more frequent than in the benign obesity-related form.
Commonly coexists with other paraneoplastic signs, notably tripe palms (palmar acanthosis) and the sign of Leser-Trelat, reflecting a shared growth-factor mechanism.
Pruritus is frequently marked, in contrast to the largely asymptomatic insulin-resistance-associated variant.
The eruption may precede, accompany or follow diagnosis of the tumour and characteristically parallels the malignancy, regressing with successful treatment and recurring with relapse.
Weight loss rather than obesity, together with rapid progression over weeks to months, helps distinguish it clinically from the common benign insulin-resistance type.
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant acanthosis nigricans is thought to arise from tumour-secreted growth factors that stimulate epidermal proliferation. Transforming growth factor alpha (TGF-alpha), which is structurally similar to epidermal growth factor and binds the epidermal growth factor receptor on keratinocytes, is considered central, with contributions from fibroblast growth factor and insulin-like growth factor 1. This drives keratinocyte and fibroblast hyperproliferation producing papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis, while relatively modest increases in melanin account for the hyperpigmented appearance. The parallel course with tumour burden supports a humoral, growth-factor-mediated aetiology rather than local insulin-receptor activation as seen in benign disease.
additionalDifferentials: Drug-induced acanthosis nigricans (nicotinic acid, systemic corticosteroids, oestrogens, protease inhibitors)
Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis of Gougerot-Carteaud
Endocrinopathy-associated acanthosis nigricans (HAIR-AN syndrome, acromegaly, Cushing syndrome)
Pellagra and other nutritional dermatoses affecting flexures
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy, given the leading association with gastric adenocarcinoma
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify an occult primary and to stage disease
Tumour markers as directed by suspected primary (CEA, CA 19-9, CA-125)
Skin biopsy demonstrating papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis with minimal hyperpigmentation
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and insulin to exclude insulin-resistance-related disease
Colonoscopy and faecal occult blood testing when a lower gastrointestinal primary is suspected
PET-CT when conventional imaging is unrevealing
redFlags: New extensive acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese adult over 40
Rapid progression with mucosal involvement and unexplained weight loss
Concurrent tripe palms or eruptive seborrhoeic keratoses
Marked pruritus with associated systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: The prognosis reflects the underlying malignancy, which is frequently an advanced, aggressive adenocarcinoma with short median survival. Cutaneous lesions may improve or regress following effective tumour treatment.
pitfalls: Attributing new acanthosis nigricans to obesity and missing an underlying tumour
Failing to examine the mucosae and palms or to look for the sign of Leser-Trelat
Assuming a normal initial endoscopy excludes malignancy when clinical suspicion is high
Overlooking recurrence of the skin signs as a marker of tumour relapse
